entities.name: Barak Khan
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Barak Khan (reigned c. 1423–1428 CE) emerged as a pivotal, albeit short-lived, figure in the fractured political landscape of the Golden Horde, representing the Jochid lineage's persistent struggle for centralized authority in the early 15th century. His rule, centered around the lower Volga and the Syr Darya regions, marked a crucial attempt to reunite the disparate uluses (domains) that had splintered after the death of Tokhtamysh and the devastating campaigns of Timur. Barak's significance lies in his audacious, though ultimately unsuccessful, efforts to reassert the Golden Horde's dominion over its former territories and influence the nascent Muscovite state, placing him at the nexus of steppe politics and emerging Russian power.

Barak Khan's ascent was characterized by brutal internal conflicts and strategic alliances. He initially gained power with the support of Ulugh Beg, the Timurid ruler of Transoxiana, leveraging this backing to defeat rivals like Kebek Khan and Muhammad Khan in a series of bloody engagements around 1423–1425. His most notable achievement was the temporary consolidation of significant portions of the Golden Horde's western and eastern wings, allowing him to challenge the growing influence of Lithuania in the west and exert pressure on Moscow. He famously raided Ryazan and negotiated with Grand Duke Vytautas of Lithuania, seeking to restore the traditional Jochid hegemony over the Rus' principalities, a policy that reflected the Golden Horde's historical claims.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Barak Khan's reign represents a critical, albeit failed, attempt to re-centralize the Golden Horde in the early 15th century, directly preceding its terminal fragmentation into successor states like the Nogai and Crimean Khanates. His actions significantly shaped the political landscape of Eastern Europe and Central Asia by accelerating the decline of a unified Mongol successor state.
